blog_summary: Adrian Colyer revisits David Parnas' 1971 classic paper, highlighting its enduring relevance to modern software development, particularly in the context of microservices and cloud-native architectures. The paper argues that the effectiveness of modularization depends critically on the criteria used to divide a system into modules. Parnas defines modules as work assignment units rather than subprograms, and outlines three key benefits: reduced development time, improved flexibility, and better comprehensibility. The paper illustrates these ideas through a case study of a KWIC index generator, comparing two decompositions—one based on workflow steps and another based on information hiding. The latter approach, which encapsulates design decisions likely to change, proves superior in isolating changes, simplifying interfaces, and improving comprehensibility, though it may introduce performance overhead. Colyer emphasizes that modern developers should pay more attention to the criteria for module boundaries, as these choices profoundly impact agility, development time, and system understanding.
paper_title: On the criteria to be used in decomposing systems into modules
